parts.label: Part 1
parts.title: Mystery Drawing
parts.subtitle: Is the drawing of a young Milanese girl really by famous artist Leonardo da Vinci?
parts.article:
Mystery Drawing

(A) On January 30, 1998, an art auction was held in New York city. One drawing was of a pretty girl, but it attracted little attention. The catalogue listed the work as a German drawing done in ink and with coloured chalk, dating back to the early 19th century, with styling borrowed from the much earlier Renaissance period. A New York dealer, Kate Ganz, purchased the picture for $21,850. The price had barely changed almost ten years later when a Canadian collector, Peter Silverman, bought it. The drawing might actually date from the Renaissance, he thought. Ganz herself had mentioned Leonardo da Vinci as an influence on the artist. Silverman wondered whether it was the work of the great Leonardo himself, but discovery of a Da Vinci is truly rare. At the time of Silverman’s purchase, it had been more than 75 years since the last authentication of one of the artist’s paintings. It had never been recorded that Da Vinci ever made a major work like this, and neither were there any known copies. If this image was an authentic Leonardo, where had it been hiding for 500 years?

(B) Silverman emailed a digital image of the drawing to Martin Kemp, professor of art history at Oxford University and renowned Leonardo scholar. Kemp immediately flew to Zurich, where Silverman kept the drawing in a bank vault. Kemp was excited and began his own investigation. He was aided by Pascal Cotte of Lumière Technology in Paris, who used high resolution multispectral scans which allowed Kemp to study the drawing’s different layers. The more Kemp looked, the more he saw what he considered evidence of Leonardo’s hand: the beautiful tone of the colours, the precise lines, and the fact that the shaded areas showed distinctive strokes just like Leonardo’s. The subject’s expression was self-confident but thoughtful. She appeared to be someone growing up too fast, and conveyed Leonardo’s belief that a portrait should reveal ‘motion of the mind’.

(C) Kemp also needed proof that the portrait had been made during Leonardo's lifetime (1452-1519) and that its historical details fitted the artist's biography. Material analysis strongly suggested that the artist had used calfskin, quite normal for the time, and this was then carbon-dated. Its origin was placed somewhere between 1440 and 1650. Then costume research revealed that the girl belonged specifically to the Milanese court of the 1490s, with its fashion for elaborately bound hair. Leonardo lived in Milan during this time, accepting commissions for portraits of people in the royal court. Stitch marks on the edge of the portrait suggested that it came from a book, possibly the sort, common at the time, that would commemorate a royal marriage.

(D) Kemp's detective work led him to a name, Bianca Sforza. A daughter of the Duke of Milan, she was married in 1496 to Galeazzo Sanseverino, commander of the Milanese troops and a patron of Leonardo's. Tragically, she died a few months later. In 2010 Kemp and Cotte published their findings in a book. Several prominent Leonardo scholars agreed, others were sceptical. The possibility of a high-quality forgery was raised. Doubt centred around the drawing’s sudden, almost miraculous appearance. Where had it come from?

(E) Kemp didn’t know. Then, quite unexpectedly, a message came from David Wright, professor of art history at the University of South Florida. Having followed the very public dispute, Wright suggested to Kemp, whom he had never met, that his answer might lie in the National Library of Poland in Warsaw, inside a book called the Sforziad. Wright, an expert on Renaissance iconography, described it as a commemorative volume for the marriage of Bianca Sforza, a suitable occasion for a Leonardo portrait.

(F) Kemp and Cotte travelled to Warsaw. Cotte’s macrophotography revealed that a page had been removed from the exact place in the Sforziad where a portrait would have been added. The moment arrived when they inserted a copy of Bianca’s portrait into the open book. It fitted perfectly. For Kemp, this was the proof. It was a single portrait by Leonardo that had gone into a book and then onto a shelf.

(G) According to Wright, the volume reached Poland in the early 1500s, when a member of the Sforza family married a Polish royal. The page was removed, possibly at the time of the book’s rebinding in the 17th or 18th century. The trail grows faint here. What is known is that at some point it was acquired by an Italian man, a specialist in art restoration, and that his widow put it up for sale at auction.

(H) These are amazing times for Leonardo admirers. Recently, London’s National Gallery exhibited Leonardo’s painting of Jesus Christ holding a globe, a work lost for centuries. In Florence, researchers looking for Leonardo’s Battle of Anghiari, last seen in the mid-1500s, are using technology to find out if the painting might be hidden behind a wall in the Palazzo Vecchio, but the issue has not yet been resolved.

(I) Authenticating a centuries-old artwork is seldom an objective process. Ego, personal taste, and fear of legal cases all contribute to the judgement. To reach wider consensus, Kemp sent his latest findings to a number of leading specialists, almost all of whom declined to comment. Agreement ‘will take time’ concedes Kemp, ‘but I have clear confidence in the research we’ve done. One thing is sure, should the day come when Bianca Sforza’s face hangs in a museum as a true Leonardo, everyone will stare.’

groups.contentHtml:
The drawing’s discovery and early research
Art dealer Kate Ganz bought a drawing of a girl made using chalk and ink.
Ganz sold the drawing to art collector Peter Silverman.
Silverman suspected the portrait was by Leonardo da Vinci but knew that
•   no new Da Vinci work had been found for over years
•   no of the portrait were believed to exist
Martin Kemp believed the drawing may be by Da Vinci because of
•   the lines and colours
•   the used in the drawing’s darker shaded areas
•   the on the girl’s face
Proof that the drawing had been done in Da Vinci’s lifetime came from
•   the age of the used as material
•   the style of the girl’s clothing and
•   the kind of the drawing had been taken from

analyses.content: 题目问超过多少年没有发现达芬奇的新作品了，对应原文明确指出距离上一次确认他的画作已经超过了75年。
你可能想填其他的数字或词，但要注意原文中直接跟在“超过（more than）”后面的具体年份数字就是75。

Silverman wondered whether it was the work of the great Leonardo himself, but discovery of a Da Vinci is truly rare. At the time of Silverman’s purchase, it had been more than 75 years since the last authentication of one of the artist’s paintings.
题目问人们认为这幅画没有什么存世，原文明确提到既没有记录他画过这样的巨作，也没有任何已知的复制品（copies）。
你可能会被前半句的“major work”干扰，但题目问的是“不存在什么（no...exist）”，对应原文后半句的“neither were there any known copies”。
It had never been recorded that Da Vinci ever made a major work like this, and neither were there any known copies.
题目问在画作阴影区域使用了什么，原文直接指出阴影区域展示了独特的笔触（strokes）。
你可能会想填“colours”或“lines”，但这两个词对应的是题干里的前两个并列项，只有“strokes”才是专门对应“阴影区域（shaded areas）”的特征。

The more Kemp looked, the more he saw what he considered evidence of Leonardo’s hand: the beautiful tone of the colours, the precise lines, and the fact that the shaded areas showed distinctive strokes just like Leonardo’s.
题目问女孩脸上有什么特征，原文提到画中人物的面部表情（expression）自信又深思熟虑。
你可能想填具体的形容词比如“self-confident”，但题目缺的是名词，而且原文的主语就是面部表情（expression）。
The subject’s expression was self-confident but thoughtful. She appeared to be someone growing up too fast, and conveyed Leonardo’s belief that a portrait should reveal ‘motion of the mind’.
题目问作为材料被使用并测试年代的是什么，原文说到材料分析表明艺术家使用了小牛皮（calfskin）并对其进行了碳十四年代测定。
你可能会误填“material”，但这只是题干中的概括提示词，真正被测定年龄的具体材料是小牛皮（calfskin）。

Kemp also needed proof that the portrait had been made during Leonardo's lifetime (1452-1519) and that its historical details fitted the artist's biography. Material analysis strongly suggested that the artist had used calfskin, quite normal for the time, and this was then carbon-dated.
题目问女孩的服装和什么东西的风格提供了证据，原文说服装研究揭示了这符合当时米兰宫廷精心编发（hair）的时尚。
你可能会被“fashion”干扰，但fashion在这里表示“时尚/风气”，真正和服装（clothing对应costume）并列的具体事物是头发（hair）。
Then costume research revealed that the girl belonged specifically to the Milanese court of the 1490s, with its fashion for elaborately bound hair.
题目问这幅画是从什么东西里取下来的，原文说画像边缘的缝线痕迹表明它来自一本书（book）。
你可能会想填“royal marriage”，但这只是修饰这本书的用途，画作本身直接掉落的来源是书（book）。
Stitch marks on the edge of the portrait suggested that it came from a book, possibly the sort, common at the time, that would commemorate a royal marriage.

groups.description:
Complete the notes.
Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER from the text for each answer.

questions.question: In 2010, there were mixed reactions to Kemp and Cotte’s research on the drawing.

analyses.content: 题目说2010年人们对他们的研究反应不一，原文提到他们2010年出书后，有些学者同意，另一些人则持怀疑态度，这完全符合“反应不一”。
你可能觉得原文没有直接出现“mixed reactions”这个词就犹豫，但这正是“有人同意、有人怀疑”的同义替换。
In 2010 Kemp and Cotte published their findings in a book. Several prominent Leonardo scholars agreed, others were sceptical.

questions.question: Kemp contacted Professor David Wright for his advice on the drawing.

analyses.content: 题目说是Kemp主动联系了Wright求建议，但原文说两人从未谋面，是Wright出乎意料地主动给Kemp发了信息并提出建议。
你可能会看到两人确实有交流就选TRUE，但千万要注意动作的发出者方向反了，不是Kemp找Wright，而是Wright主动找的Kemp。

Then, quite unexpectedly, a message came from David Wright, professor of art history at the University of South Florida. Having followed the very public dispute, Wright suggested to Kemp, whom he had never met, that his answer might lie in the National Library of Poland in Warsaw, inside a book called the Sforziad.

questions.question: An Italian art restorer attempted to restore the colour to the drawing.

analyses.content: 题目说一位意大利艺术修复师试图恢复这幅画的色彩，原文只提到了这幅画曾被一位意大利艺术修复专家买下，根本没提他有没有动手去修复颜色。
你可能会看到原文有“art restoration（艺术修复）”这个词就脑补他肯定做了修复，但文章并没有给出他实际修复画作色彩的具体行动信息。

The page was removed, possibly at the time of the book’s rebinding in the 17th or 18th century. The trail grows faint here. What is known is that at some point it was acquired by an Italian man, a specialist in art restoration, and that his widow put it up for sale at auction.

questions.question: Research has revealed the location of Da Vinci’s painting Battle of Anghiari.

analyses.content: 题目说研究已经揭示了《安吉亚里战役》这幅画的位置，原文却明确说研究人员正在找，而且“这个问题尚未解决（not yet been resolved）”。
你可能会看到原文提到研究人员在使用技术寻找就以为找到了，一定要看到句末的“尚未解决”才能判断题干的“已经揭示”是错误的。

In Florence, researchers looking for Leonardo’s Battle of Anghiari, last seen in the mid-1500s, are using technology to find out if the painting might be hidden behind a wall in the Palazzo Vecchio, but the issue has not yet been resolved.

questions.question: There has been a refusal by most Da Vinci experts to respond to Kemp’s findings.

analyses.content: 题目说大多数达芬奇专家拒绝回应Kemp的发现，原文提到他把发现发给许多顶尖专家，而“几乎所有人都不予置评（declined to comment）”，表述一致。
你可能会对“refusal”这个词感到陌生，但它就是原文“declined to comment（拒绝评论）”的同义替换。
To reach wider consensus, Kemp sent his latest findings to a number of leading specialists, almost all of whom declined to comment.

questions.question: Kemp now doubts whether the drawing was really done by Da Vinci.

analyses.content: 题目说Kemp现在怀疑这幅画到底是不是达芬奇画的，原文中Kemp却亲口说“我对我们所做的研究有明确的信心（clear confidence）”，这与怀疑截然相反。
